question: What is WebRTC?

options.B: A technology enabling real-time peer-to-peer communication (audio, video, data) in browsers

explanation: WebRTC (Web Real-Time Communication): browser API for peer-to-peer audio, video, and data. No plugins needed. Powers: video calls, screen sharing, file transfer, gaming. Direct browser-to-browser communication.

question: What makes WebRTC different from WebSockets?

options.B: WebRTC is peer-to-peer and optimized for media; WebSockets go through a server

explanation: WebRTC: peer-to-peer (direct between browsers), optimized for real-time media (adaptive bitrate, jitter buffers). WebSockets: client-server, general-purpose bidirectional. Different use cases.

question: What is a signaling server in WebRTC?

options.B: A server that helps peers discover each other and exchange connection information

explanation: Signaling server: coordinates connection setup. Exchanges: SDP (session description), ICE candidates (network paths). Not part of WebRTC spec—use WebSockets, HTTP, etc. Once connected, peers communicate directly.

question: What is ICE in WebRTC?

options.B: Interactive Connectivity Establishment—a framework for finding the best path between peers

explanation: ICE: finds network path between peers. Gathers candidates: local IP, server-reflexive (STUN), relay (TURN). Tests connectivity. Handles NAT traversal. Essential for peer-to-peer in real networks.

question: What is STUN in WebRTC?

options.B: Session Traversal Utilities for NAT—helps discover public IP and port for NAT traversal

explanation: STUN server: tells client its public IP/port (as seen from outside NAT). Client uses this for ICE candidates. Lightweight, stateless. Works when NAT allows direct connection. Free STUN servers available.

question: What is TURN in WebRTC?

options.B: Traversal Using Relays around NAT—relays traffic when direct connection isn't possible

explanation: TURN server: relays media when direct connection fails (symmetric NAT, firewalls). All traffic goes through TURN. More expensive (bandwidth), but ensures connectivity. Fallback when STUN fails.

question: What is SDP in WebRTC?

options.B: Session Description Protocol—describes media capabilities, codecs, and connection information

explanation: SDP: text format describing session. Contains: media types, codecs, encryption keys, ICE candidates. Exchanged via signaling. Offer/answer model: caller sends offer, callee sends answer. Negotiates capabilities.

question: What are common use cases for WebRTC?
explanation: WebRTC use cases: video calls (Zoom, Meet, Teams), screen sharing, P2P file transfer, online gaming, IoT communication, live streaming (low latency). Any real-time browser communication.

question: Is WebRTC encrypted?

options.B: Yes—DTLS for data channels, SRTP for media; encryption is mandatory

explanation: WebRTC security: encryption mandatory. DTLS (Datagram TLS) for data channels. SRTP (Secure RTP) for media. Keys exchanged via DTLS-SRTP. End-to-end encrypted by default. Can't disable.

question: What is a data channel in WebRTC?

options.B: A peer-to-peer channel for sending arbitrary data (text, files, game state)

explanation: Data channel: P2P data transfer. Like WebSocket but peer-to-peer. Configurable: reliable/unreliable, ordered/unordered. Use cases: chat, file transfer, game state sync. Low latency, no server relay.

question: What is the challenge of scaling WebRTC for large video conferences?

options.B: Peer-to-peer doesn't scale—need SFU or MCU servers to relay/mix streams

explanation: Scaling challenge: P2P mesh doesn't scale (n² connections). Solutions: SFU (Selective Forwarding Unit)—server relays streams, each client sends once. MCU (Multipoint Control Unit)—server mixes into one stream. Most use SFU.

question: A company wants to build a video calling feature in their web app. What technology enables this without plugins?

options.B: WebRTC—native browser support for real-time video/audio

explanation: WebRTC: native in all modern browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge). No plugins. getUserMedia for camera/mic access, RTCPeerConnection for P2P. Standard approach for browser-based video calling.
